RDC: l’Eglise catholique ne sait plus à quel saint se vouer!
items.description: En République démocratique du Congo (RDC), alors que les fidèles catholiques et leurs pasteurs s’apprêtent à célébrer, dans un mois presque jour pour jour, la naissance du petit Jésus, c’est le chemin de la croix qui précède sa mort trois jours avant sa résurrection que les forces de l’ordre leur imposent. A la place de l’encens qui les aident à chasser les mauvais esprits et à embaumer l’air, le gaz lacrymogène bien piquant, leur a été partagé à profusion par des forces de sécurité qui excellent bien dans ce genre d’exercice. Les fidèles et leurs évêques manifestaient, ce lundi 23 novembre, à Lubumbashi, pour réclamer l’exécution d’un jugement prononcé en faveur de l’Eglise dans une affaire de spoliation d’une portion de la propriété du Grand séminaire interdiocésain Saint-Paul de ladite ville. La police a si bien fait son travail que les manifestants ne savaient plus à quel saint se vouer. Pourtant, la marche, en plus d’être pacifique était…catholique, donc à priori, sans crainte de dérive. Sauf qu’elle a été interdite par la mairie. Ce qui a fait des évêques, des séminaristes et d’autres fidèles, des hors-la-loi d’un instant. Mais, sauf erreur d’appréciation de profane, comment quelques manifestants, affublés juste de crucifix et se protégeant les voies respiratoires pour ne pas se laisser suffoquer par les gaz lacrymogènes, peuvent-ils se transformer en une horde de malfaiteurs et de casseurs, prêts à détruire ce qu’ils veulent protéger? Pourquoi les forces de sécurité n’ont-elles pas plutôt cherché à encadrer cette manifestation, quitte à ce que l’édile de Lubumbashi lance par la suite une poursuite judiciaire contre les autorités diocésaines pour non-respect de la décision de la mairie? Où est donc passée cette confiance aveugle que mérite les hommes de Dieu, à qui l’on donne la communion sans confesse, au propre comme au figuré? Les interrogations pourraient s’enchaîner sans fin. Cette séance gratuite d’inhalation de gaz lacrymogènes aurait pu être évitée, peut-être si les forces de sécurité et de défense de la RDC n’étaient pas sur la braise, les doigts sur la gâchette, à cause de la guerre contre les groupes armés du Front de réconciliation de la nation (FRN) ex AFC-M23. Félix Tshisekedi très préoccupé par son dialogue national contesté et son referendum constitutionnel en vue, ne s’est-il pas ouvert un autre front inutile contre l’Eglise catholique? Certainement, surtout que la veille de l’incident de Lubumbashi, le Cardinal Fridolin Ambongo a été empêché par le pouvoir, de célébrer une messe au cours de laquelle il devait s’adresser à la jeunesse de la RDC. La rencontre entre le Cardinal devait se tenir au stade Tata Raphaël de Kinshasa qui a été ceinturée par les forces de sécurité. De quoi ont donc peur les autorités? Le Cardinal Ambongo, homme de Dieu, donc de paix allait-il monter les jeunes contre le pouvoir, par un discours de vérité? La vérité sur, entre autres, l’ambition de Félix Tshisekedi d’aller à un 3e mandat, voire un pouvoir à vie en changeant la Loi fondamentale? En tout cas, malgré le bouclage du stade, le prélat a pu parler à la jeunesse sur le terrain Saint-Raphaël, dans une école catholique: «Mes chers jeunes, gardez une foi inébranlable, même au milieu de la provocation. Refusez la violence, la haine, la corruption.» Deux petites phrases d’une prêche qui n’a point fait allusion à la révision constitutionnelle, encore moins à la guerre qui fait rage dans l’est de la RDC, mais qui ont certainement marqué une jeunesse congolaise lasse des maux qui minent leur pays et dont les politiques, portent la responsabilité. Jusqu’où ira ce que le Cardinal Fridolin Ambongo qualifie de «provocation» de la part du pouvoir? Par Wakat Séra L’article RDC: l’Eglise catholique ne sait plus à quel saint se vouer! est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Commercial loans behind UG hostel fee hikes – Vice Chancellors Ghana
items.description: The rising cost of student accommodation in Ghana’s public universities requires a national funding arrangement involving government, university authorities, students and private investors, the Executive Secretary of Vice Chancellors Ghana, Dr Cynthia Kpeglo-Freiku, has said. She said the recent controversy over hostel charges at the University of Ghana (UG) should prompt a broader examination of how tertiary institutions finance student housing, rather than be treated as an isolated dispute between university management and students. Dr Kpeglo-Freiku argued that universities faced difficult financial choices in expanding and maintaining accommodation, particularly where facilities had been developed through commercial borrowing. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, November 23, she said the University of Ghana Enterprises Limited (UGEL) was established as a commercial subsidiary to help the university generate internally generated funds and support its operations. She explained that the accommodation facilities operated by the company were part of efforts to address student housing needs at a time when universities had limited public funding to undertake such projects. According to her, institutions that resorted to bank loans to construct accommodation had to meet the commercial repayment terms, including interest, making it necessary to structure hostel charges to cover those financial obligations. She said the history of UGEL and the circumstances surrounding the construction of its facilities were important to understanding the current fee controversy. Dr Kpeglo-Freiku recalled that during an earlier period of student agitation over accommodation costs, the government had undertaken to settle some of the financial obligations associated with university projects. She said universities had to consider the cost of borrowing and the need to redeem loans to avoid defaulting on their obligations. Her comments come amid protests and disagreements over accommodation charges at the University of Ghana, where students have raised concerns about affordability and hostel conditions. For the 2026/2027 academic year, the university reduced a proposed 26 per cent increase in charges for standard four-bed rooms in its four Diaspora halls to 15 per cent following consultations with student leaders. The adjustment takes the annual accommodation fee from GH¢7,000 to GH¢8,050 per student. The university has explained that several UGEL-managed residential facilities were constructed with commercial loans secured when public funding was inadequate. It says the charges are intended to cover loan repayments, utility bills, maintenance and other operational expenses. Beyond the UG dispute Dr Kpeglo-Freiku cautioned against narrowing the accommodation debate to the University of Ghana, saying the challenges reflected wider financial pressures confronting public universities. She said the country needed to confront the fundamental question of who should bear the cost of providing decent and affordable accommodation for tertiary students. She proposed a national roundtable involving government, university authorities, students and private investors to agree on a sustainable financing model. The discussions, she said, should be conducted objectively and without allowing the emotions surrounding individual fee disputes to overshadow the broader policy questions. She also acknowledged that accommodation was only one of several difficulties facing students and universities, pointing to the wider economic pressures affecting households and institutions. The proposed national dialogue, she said, should help determine how the responsibility for financing student housing could be shared without placing an unsustainable burden on students or universities. The debate has gained urgency as universities seek to expand residential capacity while managing limited resources. The University of Ghana, for instance, has announced plans for additional hostel projects, including proposed 10,000-bed and 20,000-bed facilities in collaboration with the government. Dr Kpeglo-Freiku said a lasting solution would require stakeholders to look beyond immediate fee adjustments and address the funding arrangements needed to provide and maintain student accommodation across the tertiary sector.

items.title: Kick Nation Select depart Ghana for Surf Cup International in Spain
items.description: Ghanaian youth football side Kick Nation Select have departed the country for Spain to compete in the 2026 Surf Cup International. The team, made up of 18 players, will be hoping to use the tournament as an opportunity to test themselves against youth sides from different parts of the world and gain valuable international experience. Kick Nation Select have been drawn in Group G alongside Huesca International, IDF Valencia Royal and TNL International Select. Ahead of their departure, the team received a send-off from Minister of Education Haruna Iddrisu, who hosted the delegation at his residence. Kick Nation select delegation at residence of Minister of Education, Haruna Iddrisu Addressing the players, Mr Iddrisu urged them to remain disciplined throughout the trip and prioritise their safe return. “First of all, you are all travelling, and it is my prayer and hope that you all return. You are all footballers, and discipline is paramount in your journey,” he said. The team’s director and chief executive officer, Wunam Haruna, also highlighted the importance of the tournament to the development of the young players. He said the competition would provide an opportunity for the players to measure themselves against international opposition while showcasing their abilities to scouts and clubs. The trip forms part of Kick Nation Select’s efforts to expose young Ghanaian footballers to international competition and create opportunities for their development.

items.title: Jensen Huang and Silicon Valley’s Short-Term Thinking
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Just like that, Jensen Huang is back on top. Reportedly, President Trump called Nvidia’s board and encouraged it to reinstate the former CEO, who had been pushed out only two weeks earlier. The board made the “correct and proper decision,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, which ensures the “Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.” The president seemed happy. Tech leaders were relieved. The stock market seemed to rally with the news. A lot of other interested parties, however, still have burning questions. Lawmakers from both parties are planning to grill Huang about the affair he had with a suspected Chinese spy and the related threats to national security. But how will Americans, who just voted resoundingly against AI, data centers, and grift among the rich, receive the president giving a pass to his tech-CEO friend? On this episode of Radio Atlantic , Charlie Warzel talks about Nvidia, Huang, the short-term thinking of tech CEOs, and an economy held hostage by AI. The following is a transcript of the episode: Charlie Warzel: We just had an election where, as you alluded to, America expressed deep concern with artificial intelligence in general, with data centers, which are the thing that house all the Nvidia chips. And you have a class of new lawmakers who are coming in with a mandate from America to try to rein in this, like, tech-elite class, this AI economy that people feel is akin to a hostage situation, right? You’re gonna have, like, all of that collide in D.C., and I think it’s gonna be a nightmare. I really do. [ Music ] Hanna Rosin: Today, Jensen Huang was reinstated as chairman of Nvidia, the chip-manufacturing giant. Elon Musk posted on X, “The mistake has been corrected.” The president referred to it as the “correct and proper decision” and posted an AI-generated meme showing Huang in the same raised-fist pose that Trump himself adopted after the 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania. So for the president, for Huang, and for other tech giants: order restored. For a lot of other people, though—what? I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic . It’s been just about two weeks since Huang, who is close to the president, admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Congressional leaders are at this very moment continuing to call up Huang to testify about the dangers his affair posed to national security. The showdown with China over spying, over AI dominance, is still a looming threat of our era. And yet, there is Huang, right back in his corner office with his latest leather jacket. Joining me to discuss is tech writer and host of the Galaxy Brain podcast Charlie Warzel. Charlie, we are here once again talking about the story that never stops giving. Welcome to the show. Warzel: Thank you for having me. I told you this is the nightmare scenario two weeks ago, and here we are in the nightmare. Rosin: I knew that was my first question. So when you woke up this morning to the news that Huang was reinstated at Nvidia, do you think, No way ? Or I knew this was gonna happen. I told you so ? Warzel: Somewhere in between, honestly. It was starting to get—on Sunday, [Treasury Secretary] Scott Bessent sort of walked back a little bit. He was on—I believe on CBS—one of the morning shows, and he initially took this very strident position that the Nvidia board needed to look outside the company for leadership. And then when pressed on it again, he kind of backtracked and said, Well, you know, Jensen Huang is actually now on the outside . And so that signaled a little to me that this week could get a little crazy. I didn’t anticipate it happening this quickly, though. Rosin: I mean, there has been a lot of reporting that President Trump was involved in the decision, that he called into the Nvidia board meeting to advocate for the return of Huang. What do we know so far about the president’s involvement? Warzel: I mean, this is—I don’t know if it’s unprecedented. But this is a lot of involvement from the president of the United States in a publicly traded company’s personnel decisions to—he said he both intervened directly and indirectly, whatever indirectly means. But there were calls, supposedly. There have been communications over the recent weeks with Trump and Jensen Huang, who are cellphone buddies. It’s remarkable. The hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman said that the wisdom of the crowd has spoken , which I think is a very odd way to describe the president of the United States intervening in the workings of a corporate board. But hey, the wisdom of a crowd has spoken, I guess. Rosin: Okay, so what we know so far is that the president was probably heavily involved in the decision to return back to the top of this company someone who was implicated in a national-security scandal. So it’s not obvious why a president would intervene in that way. So let’s unpack it a little bit. One theory why Trump would intervene in this way is the economy, right? Warzel: So there’s a lot here. As we talked about on a previous episode of this, as a lot of people, including myself, have written about and reported on: Nvidia, in some ways, can be seen as , like, a load-bearing block of the global economy, right? They both power the AI boom with their chips. They also invest into the AI companies through this, like, five-layer cake that Jensen Huang helped create, the circular financing, right? So they both power the boom; they finance the boom. That makes them very critical to the global economy. There are a lot of people who argue that Jensen Huang essentially, like, is the one man whose fate determines whether the market goes up and down. Nvidia stock for a while was down, but the rest of the economy was doing okay. It was kind of shouldering this. And then late last week, there was a pretty big sell-off led by a lot of tech stocks. And a lot of the year’s gains in the S&P 500 were lost. So people were kind of freaking out. I think it’s also no coincidence that this was announced—Huang’s reinstatement came—just, you know, right before the markets opened on Monday, after this huge sell-off on Friday. So the economy is a big part of this. Donald Trump believes, according to all the reporting that we’ve seen, that Jensen Huang is a critical part of the AI boom, which is, you know, propping up the rest of the stock market. Rosina: So it’s not just that Nvidia is too big to fail. It too much of a risk. It’s Jensen Wang, specifically? Warzel: That’s the belief. I mean, that’s at least what a lot of these tech leaders are saying too. So there’s really, like, three cohorts that have been agitating for this. One is Nvidia shareholders, who, obviously, Jensen Huang has made them tons and tons of money, especially if you’ve been a shareholder for a very long time in the company. But even anyone who got in after the ChatGPT revolution has seen huge gains, a stock split. So they want this guy back because he’s made them a lot of money. Then you have the Silicon Valley–elite class. I would argue the Silicon Valley–elite class wants this because they want the AI boom to continue. They have a lot riding on this. All the AI CEOs have a whole bunch of investments of their own that are predicated on all the numbers going up and up and up. But also, I think, there’s a cultural reason for this, which is: They do not want to see arguably the greatest visionary, the most irreplaceable CEO in Silicon Valley ousted, because it means that they could be ousted. It means that the CEO is vulnerable, that the visionary founder is vulnerable. I think that’s, like, a very big part of this. This is one of the existential crises that these guys have been going through, because everyone thought that Jensen was too big to fail. The fact that he had to resign after all this pressure and the board didn’t want him back is, I think to them, a very, very scary proposition because it means they can no longer act with impunity. So that was one of the reasons. And then I think you have Donald Trump, who wanted the economy to keep going on his watch, and this was the thing, the lever he thought he could pull to make number go up. Rosin: So it’s like there’s a Silicon Valley myth of a genius, and Trump has used the word genius recently. And that’s a cultural trope, but it’s also real because it drives the stock market. So it’s kind of a circular logic around this word visionary and genius that you just mentioned. Warzel: Yeah, I mean, I think that so much of stock markets, it’s a confidence game. And I don’t mean that in the sense of: It’s a con. I mean, it’s about having confidence in the market, having confidence in the direction of things. For so long, we have been talking about the economy as being propped up by AI, and we’ve been talking about AI in America as having all this very peculiar circular financing, about Is this a bubble? Is this not a bubble? And there’s this idea around all of it of extreme precarity, right? That all of this is contingent on a big bet that has been made, both about the technology succeeding but also about all of this different type of financing and all this historic investment actually meaning something and going somewhere. You need confidence from all of these investors, from all of these folks. Jensen Huang is somebody who, for this class of people, projected a lot of confidence and instilled a lot of confidence in the direction of where the economy and where the AI boom is going. So with him out of it, there was a lot of uncertainty. We were starting to see that in the markets. This freaked a lot of people out. Rosin: Right, and they don’t like uncertainty. Okay, let me run another Trump motivation by you. Lately, Trump has been talking about Alice Huang—the woman who Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with and who U.S. intelligence officials are suspecting to be a spy—has been sort of diminishing her role. He said recently, “Every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good-looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy.” Now we’ve heard this from the president, not from U.S. intelligence officials. And I was wondering if there’s something in here about Trump minimizing affairs because of his own history, sort of minimizing the importance of this kind of scandal taking down a great leader. Warzel: I think it’s not only just Trump; it’s all these folks we’re talking about in Silicon Valley. They’ve all been approaching this scandal not from the geopolitical angle of this, but from the moral-infidelity angle, right? Saying, you know, Everyone has their foibles; everyone is flawed; geniuses can be flawed too. Everyone deserves a second chance . And it’s really not a question about morality. There’s obviously, you know, the corporate-HR level of things, which is that there’s been reporting about Huang having affairs with employees in the company, including a direct report. Alice Huang was also a client of Nvidia’s, of Jensen Huang, so there’s an impropriety there. But that’s not the thing that people, that lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are upset about right now. They’re upset about the fact that Alice Huang has this alleged tie to Chinese intelligence, and what, if anything, this did to the larger geopolitical question: whether Megaspeed, this company she worked with, was skirting U.S. chip-export bans, allowing Nvidia chips to get into China or to be used by China in these remote-access data centers; or whether or not Alice Huang was reporting on things that Jensen Huang was doing; whether she had access to any of his devices or anything like that—all of those geopolitical concerns. So it’s interesting to watch both Trump and all these executives sort of not talk about that, and just focus on this other morality play. But I think what we know is actually very troubling. There’s good evidence to suggest that a lot of chip-smuggling was going on. We don’t know whether Huang and Nvidia were directly related to this, but we know that Megaspeed certainly had some role to play in this ecosystem. And Megaspeed, it should be said, has declined all allegations of wrongdoing here. And The New York Times reported on Sunday that Alice Huang had been keeping in touch with an agent in the Chinese intelligence service for over a year. She’d been speaking with this person and staying in contact with them while she was maintaining this relationship with Jensen Huang. So that’s a lot of time. And it’s very interesting to see that report come out on Sunday and have him get reinstated on Monday. [ Music ] Rosin: When we come back, we talk about how this is more than just an economic story. [ Break ] Rosin: So right now, at this moment, there are two camps. There’s the President Trump–Jensen Huang tech-leader camp. They want Jensen Huang to come back. But the other track, which is the national-security track, is continuing to move forward. Congressional leaders are still asking Jensen Huang to come and testify. And polls show that Americans actually do care about the national-security risks involved here. So presumably, the story—you and I are gonna be talking about this again. This story is not going to go away. Let’s take the congressional testimonies first. What does it look like if you have Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, testifying before Congress with the president’s backing—as opposed to what could have been, which is Jensen Huang, a citizen, not beholden to the company, not the CEO, and without the support of the president? Warzel: In an interesting way, this is just a way bigger scandal now. Like, this is a way bigger, thornier, more intense, more interesting scandal. Which, again, if you’re Donald Trump—and, also, people who care about, you know, Nvidia’s relationship to the global economy and the AI boom—the logic doesn’t fully make sense there, right? You would probably want this to go away rather than become, like, the central story of Washington, D.C., for the next 12 months or so. It remains to be seen whether Huang will just come there and plead the Fifth, right? Just say, like, absolutely nothing because basically anything he could say seems like it may or may not jeopardize Nvidia’s position, a bunch of other people. He is now in charge of this company. It’s also going to absolutely invigorate the investigations, again, which you’re seeing are coming from both China hawks or just people who are very upset about the way that this has been handled by the Trump administration and Trump’s involvement in getting him reinstated. I sort of don’t have words for how charged this is going to be. We just had an election where, as you alluded to, America expressed deep concern with artificial intelligence in general, with data centers, which are the thing that house all the Nvidia chips. And you have a class of new lawmakers who are coming in with a mandate from America to try to rein in this, like, tech-elite class, this AI economy that people feel is akin to a hostage situation, right? You have all of these people saying, If you don’t let us build what we wanna do and act the way that we wanna do, then the numbers gonna go down. All this, you know—the bubble’s gonna pop, and good luck, right? Nice economy you got there; hope nothing happens to it , sort of situation. You’re gonna have, like, all of that collide in D.C., and I think it’s gonna be a nightmare. I really do. Rosin: Yeah, that’s absolutely correct because if there is one desire from this midterm flip, it’s accountability. Like, let us enter an era of accountability where rich people don’t get to get away with whatever they want to get away with. That’s what the people seem to be asking for, both in their concerns about corruption, their concerns about data centers, everything that you just mentioned. And this just feels like a sort of pushback to all that. Warzel: Absolutely. And I think that a lot of people are gonna have stuff to prove here, right? They’re gonna wanna make an example out of all of this. And I was talking to somebody in Silicon Valley this morning about this, and they were saying to me that the election really showed this really short-term political thinking, right? The tech leaders were so focused on the AI bet that they allowed themselves to get caught up in, you know, hitching their wagon to Trump and the MAGA situation, right? Like, all the donations for the ballroom, the standing behind him at the inauguration, all of the meetings, the fawning, and all of that. And not seeing that the political winds could blow, you know, in other directions, that hitching your star to this guy so completely was a bad calculation. It’s because they had this short-term thinking. And this person described this to me as, like, another perfect example of the short-term thinking. Like, yes, we solved this problem in the very near term. The stock market is gonna rally now on all of this. But what’s it gonna mean for this to become a far bigger political scandal? Like, what is that going to mean potentially to, you know, how the Democrats are going to position themselves against AI in 2028? Like, it seems like they are playing checkers instead of, you know, the seven-dimensional chess that they always claim to be playing. Rosin: Yeah. Well, Charlie, it looks like there’s gonna be a showdown, and I look forward to talking to you about it when it unfolds. Thank you so much for explaining this to us. Warzel: Yeah. Absolutely. Happy to be here. Rosin: That is all for today’s show. [ Music ] Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered by Miguel Carrascal and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of podcasts, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. If you like what you saw here today, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can find them on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page. You can find them on Apple or Spotify or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And you can subscribe to this publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Until next time, I’m Hanna Rosin.

items.title: India: Modi Rule Has Weakened Democratic Institutions
items.description: Click to expand Image A student, participating in a protest led by the Cockroach Janta Party, holds a poster that reads “Whenever Modi is Afraid, He Pushes the Police to the Forefront,” in New Delhi, India, July 22, 2026. © 2026 Anindito Mukherjee/Bloomberg via Getty Images Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government has systematically weakened institutions established to protect human rights and democratic freedoms.Over the past decade, the Modi government has eroded the rule of law and promoted Hindu majoritarianism, rolling back human rights protections, undermining the rights of marginalized communities, and deepening India’s authoritarian slide.The government should stop using state institutions as weapons against its critics and instead use them to safeguard everyone’s rights. India’s allies should press the Modi government to restore checks on executive power. (London) – Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government has systematically weakened institutions established to protect human rights and democratic freedoms, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. Indians have increasingly taken to the streets to protest government repression, corruption, and a deeply flawed revision of voter lists. The 95-page report, “‘So What’s This Democracy We’re Talking About?’: Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India,” finds that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government is undermining parliamentary procedures, suppressing the political opposition, and weaponizing federal investigative agencies for political ends. Human Rights Watch found that the government is also weakening constitutional and statutory bodies, such as the Election Commission, Central Information Commission, the anti-corruption ombudsman, and human rights commissions, and interfering in the judicial branch. November 23, 2026 “So What’s This Democracy We’re Talking About?” Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India Download the full report in English “Over the past decade, the Modi government has been hollowing out India’s independent institutions that are critical to checking executive power and protecting civil liberties,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The government has eroded the rule of law and promoted Hindu majoritarianism, rolling back human rights protections, undermining the rights of marginalized communities, and deepening India’s authoritarian slide.” Human Rights Watch interviewed over 40 lawyers, journalists, activists, researchers, academics, current and former judges, and former government officials between January 2025 and September 2026. The Modi administration has frequently disregarded parliamentary oversight mechanisms to impose its political agenda. In December 2023, the government adopted a law that entrenched executive control over the appointment of election commissioners and granted them sweeping legal immunity for actions, decisions, or statements made while carrying out their official duties. The law was passed even as opposition members were suspended in unprecedented numbers from both houses for the entire session of the parliament, 100 from Lok Sabha (the House of the People or lower house) and 46 from Rajya Sabha (the Council of States or upper house). The BJP did not have a majority in the Rajya Sabha from 2014 to 2024. While all bills must be approved by both houses to become law, some regulating financial matters can be introduced in the Lok Sabha as “money bills,” which do not require Rajya Sabha approval. The Modi administration aggressively used money bills to push through laws with serious consequences for fundamental rights that would not qualify as money bills. In 2019, the government used this approach to amend the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, significantly expanding the authority of the Enforcement Directorate, the federal enforcement agency it has used to improperly target political opponents, activists, and critics. The expansion of Enforcement Directorate powers would not appear to fall within the parameters set out for a money bill. The Election Commission has repeatedly failed to hold Modi and senior BJP leaders to account despite apparent violations of the election code of conduct by use of hate speech. The commission has also failed to credibly investigate allegations by voters, activists, academics, and political parties of manipulation of registered voter lists, suppression of polling data, irregularities in counting votes, or interfering with voting machines. The commission is currently facing a massive crisis of credibility amid concerns over its ability to function independent of the executive. A Special Intensive Revision, purportedly to delete dead, duplicate, or ineligible voters, has arbitrarily removed over 130 million names from electoral rolls since June 2025, sparking nationwide protests in October 2026. The administration has used federal agencies to pressure members of rival parties to defect to the BJP. After amending the law against money laundering, official data shows that the Enforcement Directorate filed cases against 193 politiciansbetween April 2015 and February 2025, most of whom were government opponents. This was more than a 600 percent jump from the 26 politicians investigated in the decade preceding the Modi administration. Such investigations are promptly stalled, or charges are dropped if the accused switches loyalties, leading opposition parties to call the BJP a “washing machine.” The Modi government has since 2014 increasingly used federal investigation agencies to target domestic and international rights groups, human rights lawyers, activists, and media organizations under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Actand other laws dealing with financial irregularities. It has used the abusive counterterrorism law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), to wrongfully jail human rights activists, journalists, students, peaceful protesters, academics, and critics, sometimes for years without trial. India’s courts have also failed to uphold fundamental freedoms. In 2022, the Supreme Court endorsed and expanded the authority of enforcement agencies for arrest and search and seizure under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. Legal scholars criticized the verdict as gutting rights to life and liberty. The Supreme Court is currently hearing petitions regarding the legitimacy of the electoral roll revision process. In May 2026, even after millions of names had been eliminated from voter lists, the court ruled that the data did not indicate “systemic disenfranchisement.” In April, after 9 million names—12 percent of the electorate—in West Bengal state had been removed, the court effectively said it was acceptable for them not to vote at that time so long as they would be added back to the rolls. Shortly afterward, the BJP won control of the state for the first time. By November, the Election Commission, after protests, started reversing some of the decisions that had led to the arbitrary removal of names. The Modi administration’s actions over the past decade are not isolated institutional failures but mutually reinforcing elements of an authoritarian playbook, Human Rights Watch said. A weakened opposition has fewer means to resist laws that entrench executive control. Institutions led by political appointees, such as the federal and state human rights commissions, have not adequately responded to efforts to prevent the silencing of civil society. When courts fail to provide timely and effective remedies, these abuses go unchecked. India’s allies should publicly and privately raise concerns about ongoing abuses and the deterioration of democratic institutions, including during high-level engagements and interactions, at the United Nations Human Rights Council, and in negotiations for bilateral trade and security agreements. “Checking India’s democratic decline means ending the use of state institutions as weapons against government critics and rebuilding them as safeguards for everyone’s rights,” Pearson said. “India’s allies should press the Modi government to end its assault on independent institutions and restore checks on executive power.”

items.title: Herbal medicine under threat from chemical spraying, land destruction
items.description: Mr Joshua Appiah-Kubi of Poget Herbal has expressed concern over the negative impact of indiscriminate chemical spraying by farmers and the activities of illegal miners on medicinal plants used in herbal medicine production. He said the indiscriminate application of weedicides and pesticides on farms often affected nearby medicinal plants, contaminating them and rendering them unsafe for medicinal use. In an interview with the Ghana News Agency, Mr Appiah-Kubi noted that many valuable medicinal plants had been adversely affected by such practices, posing a threat to the herbal medicine industry. He further expressed concern about the invasion of farmlands and forest areas by illegal miners, whose activities were destroying large tracts of land where medicinal plants naturally thrived. According to him, activities such as deep excavations, indiscriminate felling of trees and the pollution of water bodies with mercury, cyanide and other harmful chemicals were having devastating effects on medicinal plant resources. Mr Appiah-Kubi said the continued destruction of these natural resources could undermine the availability of herbs used in traditional medicine and negatively affect public health. He, therefore, appealed to farmers to adopt responsible chemical application practices and urged illegal miners to desist from destroying forest reserves and other lands rich in medicinal plants. He stressed the need to protect the country’s medicinal plant resources, safeguard public health and preserve an important part of Ghana’s natural heritage for future generations.

items.title: Burkina/11-Décembre 2026: l’aspect festif laisse place à la célébration
items.description: Le Général de Brigade, Théophile Nikièma, Président du Comité national d'Organisation (PCO) du 11 décembre 2026, fête nationale commémorant la proclamation de l’indépendance du Burkina Faso, autrefois Haute-Volta, le 11 décembre 1958, a donné les grandes lignes de l’évènement aux hommes et femmes de médias, ce lundi 23 novembre 2026, à Ouagadougou. L’officier supérieur militaire a déclaré que pour cette édition de «relance, il ne s'agit plus d'une fête mais d'une célébration», appelant les Burkinabè de l'intérieur et de la diaspora à prendre part à cette célébration dans «l'ordre et la discipline». Le gouvernement burkinabè a décidé de renouer cette année avec la célébration nationale du 11 décembre, date de la proclamation de l’indépendance du pays. Pour cette édition de «relance», le thème est: «Révolution Progressiste Populaire au Burkina Faso : une consécration des résistances à la domination coloniale et à l'impérialisme». Après un arrêt de cinq ans, la cérémonie officielle marquant le 11 décembre, reprend sous une autre forme mais toujours dans la solennité. Face aux représentants des médias le lundi 23 novembre 2026, l’équipe chargée de l’organisation de l’évènement a tenu une première conférence de presse-annonce de la manifestation dans la Salle des Conférences internationales de Ouaga 2000. L’accent est surtout mis cette année sur le défilé miliaire et paramilitaire dans les chefs-lieux des régions. Le Président du Comité national d'Organisation (PCO) du 11-Décembre 2026, le Généra de Brigade Théophile Nikièma (micros) «Le 11 décembre 1958, la République de Haute-Volta était proclamée. Le 5 août 1960, notre pays accédait à l'indépendance. Ces dates portent la mémoire des échecs et des succès des générations qui nous ont légué cette chère Patrie. Avec la Révolution d'août 1983, le Camarade Capitaine Thomas Sankara a donné à cet héritage une exigence concrète, celle de compter sur nos propres forces pour enraciner notre pays dans la souveraineté. La Révolution Progressiste Populaire (RPP), conduite par son guide, le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, perpétue aujourd'hui cette exigence», a rappelé le Président du Comité national d’Organisation (PCO), le Général de Brigade Théophile Nikikèma. «Les choses évoluent depuis 2022 dans le sens positif bien-sûr. Il y a des choses qui se font aujourd’hui et qui était inimaginables il y a cinq à six ans. Tout ce qui se fait au Burkina Faso est décidé au Burkina Faso. C’est déjà le début de l’indépendance. Ce n’était pas vraiment le cas. Je pense que vous êtes bien placés pour le comprendre que nous sommes dans cette dynamique de reconquérir notre souveraineté totale», a soutenu l'adjoint du Chef d'état-major général des armées (CEMGA), le Général de Brigade, Théophile Nikièma. Cette volonté de souveraineté s'affirme aussi à l'échelle du Sahel. Avec les peuples frères du Mali et du Niger, le Burkina Faso a choisi, au sein de la Confédération des États du Sahel, d'assumer sa sécurité, de définir ses priorités de développement et de disposer librement de ses ressources. «Dans un monde où les rivalités de puissance s'accentuent, l'avènement de la Confédération AES donne une expression politique à une aspiration qui grandit en Afrique et au-delà, celle de peuples résolus à s'affranchir des rapports de domination et à choisir librement leurs partenaires», a indiqué le Général Théophile Nikièma. Pour cette édition du 11-Décembre, trois types d'activités majeures ainsi que des activités connexes sont au programme de la célébration. Il s’agit de la cérémonie officielle essentiellement marquée par une parade à Ouagadougou et dans tous les autres Chefs-lieux de Régions ; une série de conférences thématiques à travers le territoire national et des projections populaires de films sur les Forces de Défense et de Sécurité (FDS) et sur les résistances à la domination coloniale. Au titre de la cérémonie officielle, «c'est une grande parade militaire et paramilitaire d'envergure inédite et jamais réalisée par nos troupes, aussi bien en termes d'effectifs qu'en moyens logistiques», a affirmé le PCO face aux journalistes. Pour ce qui concerne Ouagadougou, elle se déroulera le 11 décembre 2026 sur l'Avenue Pascal-Zagré à Ouaga 2000, à partir de 09 heures 00 minute. «Le volet développement sera mis en exergue avec la participation des structures et entités émanant des Initiatives Présidentielles dans le défilé motorisé. Toutefois, cette cérémonie sera marquée dans les autres Régions par un défilé militaire et paramilitaire uniquement», a précisé l’adjoint du Chef d’état-major général des armées (CEMGA) qui a ajouté que cette «grande parade se veut une démonstration grandeur nature de la détermination de notre pays à défendre son intégrité et sa liberté de décision face à toute menace, d'où qu'elle vienne». Au titre des conférences publiques, elles porteront sur le thème de la célébration. «La conférence publique inaugurale est prévue pour le 02 décembre 2026 dans la Salle des Conférences Internationales de Ouaga 2000. Elle sera suivie par les conférences régionales dans la période du 02 au 07 décembre 2026. Au titre des projections populaires de films, l’activité va consister à projeter à des lieux publics (espaces ouverts, salle de cinéma, garnison, etc.) des films relatifs à la défense du territoire national et aux résistances anticoloniales. On peut citer le documentaire de reconstitution historique « Kidiga », ainsi que d'autres films inédits en cours de production. Présentation du visuel du 11-Décembre 2026 A côté de ces trois types d'activités majeures, il est prévu des activités connexes à savoir: un cross populaire suivi d'un méga aérobic à la date du mardi 08 décembre 2026 à Ouagadougou. Ainsi, « le 10 décembre, nous aurons une campagne de consultations médicales gratuites et une campagne de délivrance de Cartes d'identité AES dans toutes les Régions puis la cérémonie de clôture du Tournoi de la relance de l'Office de Liaison de l'Afrique de l'Ouest (OLAO) à Ouagadougou. Le Message du Camarade Président du Faso, Chef de l'Etat (Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré) est également attendu le 10 décembre à 20 heures 00 minute», a informé le général de brigade Théophile. Il a insisté auprès des hommes et femmes des médias et de la communication que le 11 décembre fait son grand retour surtout avec une nouvelle identité, une nouvelle charte graphique. En effet, un nouveau logotype exprimant la «fierté retrouvée d'un Peuple qui assume son histoire et exerce sa souveraineté» accompagne cette célébration nationale. Les conférenciers ont invité les Burkinabè de l'intérieur du pays et de la diaspora à prendre part activement à cette célébration dans «l'ordre et la discipline». Par Bernard BOUGOUM L’article Burkina/11-Décembre 2026: l'aspect festif laisse place à la célébration est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: 59 Ekwueme varsity students bags first class says VC
items.description: …….Honours Enerst Ndukwe, ABC Orjiakor, Francis Fatona on Convocation By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki No fewer than 59 students of Alex Ekwueme Federal University of Ndufu-Alike Ikwo (AE-FUNAI), Ebonyi State have bagged first class for the four sets of 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 academic years for first degrees. The Vice Chancellor of the University Professor Daniel Nwachukwu who disclosed this during Pre-Covocation press conferenc for 9th, 10th, 11th and 12th combined convocation, said that a total of 8,649 students would be graduating. He noted that the 1, 867 students obtained Second Class Upper Division while 5,040 students got Second Class Lower Division and 1, 675 students received Thrid Class also 8 students obtained Pass. The VC said that a total of 552 postgraduate students would be graduating across various disciplines as follows PhD (44), M.Sc. (348) and PGD (160) Professor Nwachukwu who is organizing his first convocation ceremony on November 28, 2026 having been appointed the fourth Vice Chancellor of the University ten months ago said he had brought many innovation to the institution within the short period in office. “According to the programme of activities: “Wednesday, 25th November, 2026: Research and Innovation Faire  We will showcase the research and groundbreaking innovations of our academics to the public. This underscores the contributions of our university to the betterment of society and the body of knowledge. “Thursday, 26th November, 2026: Alumni Dinner & Price Giving Day: We will host the alumni, who are critical partners to the development of our university to a dinner. At the event, prices will also be given to graduating students that distinguished themselves in their various fields/discipline, and other aspects of human endeavours. “Friday, 27th November, 2026: Chancellor’s Ball: We will host our highly-revered Chancellor, the Alake and Paramount Ruler of Egbaland, HRM Oba (Dr.) Michael Aremu Adedotun Gbadebo CFR. It will be an evening of songs and cultural display to celebrate the Chancellor. “On Saturday, 28th November, 2026, Convocation Lecture: To be delivered by Dr. ABC Orjiakor, Pioneer Chairman, Seplat Energies Ltd, with topic: ‘Who Will Build the Nigeria We Want? Character, Competence and Opportunities in a Difficult Economy’ he stated. The VC said that the university will confer Honorary Doctorate Degrees (Honoris Causa) to three eminent Nigerians for their unparallel contributions to the development of Nigeria in various areas. “The nominees are; Dr. Ernest Ndukwe, Chairman, MTN, Nigeria to be awarded with Doctor of Telecommunications Engineering (honoris causa); Dr. ABC Orjiakor, Pioneer Chairman, Seplat Energies Ltd, to be awarded with Doctor of Business Administration (honoris causa), and Dr. Olayiwola Francis Fatona, Founder Renaissance Energy to be awarded Doctor of Business Administration (honoris causa). “I assumed office as the 4th substantive Vice-Chancellor of the University on February 11, 2026 with the vision of making AE-FUNAI a hub of academic and intellectual excellence. In the last 10 months, we have hit the ground running. We have consolidated the gains of the past, while also making some sweeping changes geared towards repositioning the university. Some of the gains include: “We have instituted democratic governance in the Faculties and College of Medical Sciences, while also decentralizing administration to the Faculties. We have granted semi autonomous status to the College of Medical Sciences “We have established 14 new programmes across 5 Faculties to meet 21st century demands. These include Hotel Management and Tourism; Zoology, Environmental Biology, and Plant Science and Biotechnology; Urban and Regional Planning, Estate Management, Surveying and Geoinformatics, and Quantity Surveying; as well as Physiotherapy, Optometry, and Medical Radiography. Others are Marketing, Social Work, and Library and Information Science. “To expand access to university education and offer academic degrees to willing students, we have established academic affiliations with Marist Polytechnic, Enugu, AE-FUTHA College of Nursing, Abakaliki, Royal College of Nursing Ezzangbo, Mater Misericordia College Afikpo, and CSMT School of Biblical Studies Abakaliki, and partnership with Shandong University, Jianzhu, China, on staff and students exchange programme. “We have renovated the University Staff School, VCs office and Conference room, senate chambers, among others “About 150 solar street lights have been installed from the Main Gate to the Senate Building and College of Medical Sciences through the support of Hon. Nkemkanma Kama. We have also procured additional 200 solar street light which are been mounted across the campus. “A MoU was signed with AG-Zara for new student hostels. Senator Onyekachi Nwebonyi pledged a N250M Faculty of Law Auditorium, while Hon. Iduma Igariwey pledged a massive building project. Hon. Chinedu Ogah has also pledged a CBT Centre for the University. Further, a Renewed Hope Hostel is also been constructed in the University. “The University is at an advanced stage of discussion with a private investor for the building of a water processing industrial plant to provide portable water within and outside the campus. The plant will also provide hands-on research activities for staff and students. ” We have a proposal from a private investor for the establishment of a 21st century self-funded inter and intra campus transportation scheme using electric vehicles at no cost to the university. “Collaborations with INNOSON Motors and Zobis Wires & Cables for research, internships, and technology transfer has been consummated. “We signed a partnership with Laudable Insurance Brokers Ltd for a Students Personal Accident Insurance and Combined Risk Insurance Policy to protect our students and the university physical infrastructure. “We secured funding from TETFund and renovated the auditoriums of Faculty of Physical Sciences and Faculty of Biological Sciences. It is over 80% completed. We are revisiting the long abandoned Central Administrative building and the main library by TETFund” Prof Nwachukwu stated. items.title: Flights cancelled in Belgium due to cost-of-living strike
items.description: Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures. All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem and at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair. Underground services have also been halted in the capital, Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march. The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate. No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) due to the air traffic controllers’ strike. “In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers,” Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said. Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China’s capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled. “Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn’t even collect it,” she said. A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as “scheduled”, regardless of the time of departure or arrival. One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport. Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels. “Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that,” he told Reuters. Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions. Large numbers of people have descended on Brussels for a protest march The Belgian prime minister leads a five-party coalition. One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and cut fewer pensions and health-sector spending. De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse. “While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible,” the royal palace said in a statement. The leader of one of the country’s main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to “dismantling the social protection system”. Bert Engelaar, the union’s head, called for “a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes”. “Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It’s about knowing when to stop,” he added, praising the Vooruit party. Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised the government’s plans to cut bank holidays that fall on weekends.

items.title: Dad who discovered daughter’s murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
items.description: Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook. It was August and he hadn’t been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn’t unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time. Then one Saturday, two of Tuku’s neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured. “When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle,” says Tuku, 50. After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa’s KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country. But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn’t until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle’s body. When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten. “It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it.” Okuhle’s father, Tuku, says he feels “ignored and unseen” by the government after his daughter’s death Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student. She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September , according to the South African Police Service. Overall, there were 5,590 murders – 204 fewer than in the same period last year. It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years. There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer. South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide – the intentional killing of a woman or girl – in the world. In response to this summer’s killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas. But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands. For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter’s killing himself. Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested. “It was just silent after we buried Okuhle – there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate.” He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says. The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received. The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be “greater efforts” to prevent violence against women and children. The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing. This year, Amnesty International said South Africa’s police service was “under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence”. Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads. Despite Ramaphosa’s promises, he has little faith anything will change. “I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us.” Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February’s budget to deal with gender-based violence. Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years “and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing”. Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00 Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad. Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases. In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children. Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00. Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them. The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu. Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up. Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers. “With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there’s nothing we can do.” Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets. Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park. She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction. When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her. “Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger,” says Kgothatso, who is now 35. Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid. She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life. Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner. In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers. She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn’t met before at work. Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa. Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, “particularly in isolated areas” – after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo. She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later . It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa’s running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women’s running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events. Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth’s disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end. Zonke and Zama’s group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group. “We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing,” says Zama, 37. Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country. Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed. Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march. Wiping away tears, she said: “To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone.”

items.title: US rapper Don Toliver postpones two arena shows after Manchester evacuation
items.description: US rapper Don Toliver has postponed two London shows this week after his Manchester concert on Sunday was evacuated when an “unknown substance” was released into the crowd. Toliver was due to play The O2 on Monday and Wembley Arena on Tuesday, but Live Nation said his “stage and production equipment remains in Manchester and cannot be moved in time”. One person was taken to hospital and 89 people showed “symptoms believed to be linked to the exposure” after Sunday’s Co-op Live arena show, police said. Fans described “distressing scenes” with people “choking”, “screaming” and “coughing up blood” because of the effects of a substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas. The Wembley show has been rescheduled to 14 December, while Monday night’s O2 gig has been moved to 15 December. “I’m very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to (the) unfortunate incident last night,” Don Toliver wrote on Instagram. Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident on Sunday and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena. One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment and treatment after the incident, which happened at about 22:00 GMT, the force said. A further 88 people “underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were subsequently accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed”, according to GMP. Leon Douzi said he was right next to where the substance was released, and described someone holding a can and “this gas coming out”. “It just hit me in the throat,” he said, adding that it felt like “burning”. There was “a bit of panic”, Douzi said: “Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out.” Some fans reported eye and respiratory symptoms, according to the North West Ambulance Service. Hannah Baxter, who went to the concert with her partner, said the first thing she noticed was a burning feeling in her throat. “[We] were just coughing and coughing… there was a guy next to us who had vomited. There were people with red eyes and… tears everywhere,” she told the BBC. Joey Howe, a football journalist at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester there was a “horrible smell” and added: “People were coming through in wheelchairs choking – it was really distressing.” Police launched an investigation and are continuing to carry out tests on items at the venue to try to identify the substance. No arrests have been made. Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: “Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk. Testing will take place throughout the day as the investigation into the cause of this incident progresses. “We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident.” Some fans complained about security and a lack of searches as people went into the Manchester concert. Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were “crying and screaming in pain” as they left the venue, adding she felt “confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size”. Malachi Clarke also claimed security was “not good at all”, adding: “They weren’t checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine.” Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while “some of these are visible, others you won’t be able to see”. It said the arena used a “frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets”. Figen Murray, the mother of a Manchester Arena attack victim who led the campaign for a new law to prevent terrorist attacks at public venues, said people should feel “assured” about security measures. “A lot of the big venues use mass screening technology, where you don’t even know you’ve been checked,” she told the BBC. They also have staff observing CCTV, security guards and plain-clothed officers on site. Murray said that while the current technology is “good enough”, it needed improvement over the next few years to become “more sophisticated”. Venues are currently focused on keeping out items – such as explosives – that could cause mass casualties, she added. All fans at the Manchester show will get a full refund, promoter Live Nation said. A statement said: “We are sorry to everyone affected by last night’s events in Manchester and full refunds for that show will be automatically processed to ticket holders.” There have apparently been similar incidents earlier on Toliver’s tour, when some fans reported spray or gas being released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris. In his post on Monday, the rapper said: “I just wanna make sure everyone is safe and the next show goes on properly. My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured last night.” “The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans,” Toliver said, asking people to stop bringing substances into his shows. “It ain’t cool,” added the rapper, who was nominated for five Grammy Awards earlier this month. “See you soon London, love you Guys. DT.” Toliver’s Nitrous tour, named after his new album, is also due to visit Wembley Arena in London on Tuesday. No update has been given about that show. It was set to be the last gig of his world tour before he took a break from the road ahead of a Coachella appearance next spring. Toliver is best known for singles such as No Idea and After Party, from his debut studio album, Heaven or Hell (2020), which was big on TikTok. He also featured on Travis Scott’s song Can’t Say, from his third studio album Astroworld.

items.title: 2027: Ebonyi PDP candidate Odii promises 180,000 jobs
items.description: By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki The governorship candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Ebonyi State, Chief Ifeanyi Chukwuma Odii, has promised to create more than 180,000 jobs and introduce free public primary and secondary education if elected governor in 2027. Odii made the pledges while unveiling his 2027 governorship manifesto, titled “ANYI G’EMEYA”: A Promise of Possibility, which outlines his proposed development agenda for the state. The manifesto contains plans to transform the state’s economy through industrialisation, agricultural development and private-sector investment, while reducing its dependence on federal allocations. It identifies economic development and industrialisation, infrastructure, youth and human capital development, institutional reforms and security as key pillars of the proposed administration. On economic development, Odii said his administration would prioritise agriculture, manufacturing, trade and commerce, mining and quarrying, and tourism to create employment and expand the state’s revenue base. He proposed moving agriculture from subsistence production to commercial and technology-driven farming through mechanisation, improved farming inputs, irrigation, affordable financing and stronger market linkages. The manifesto also proposes the establishment of special agro-industrial processing zones and clusters in strategic locations to encourage large-scale processing, reduce post-harvest losses and increase the value of agricultural produce. It further identifies an initial 400 to 500 hectares of suitable land for commercial farming and agro-industrial investments, subject to feasibility assessments and consultations with host communities. Smallholder farmers, according to the document, would be integrated into the proposed investments through outgrower schemes. In the manufacturing sector, the PDP candidate promised to establish industrial clusters and manufacturing hubs equipped with electricity, access roads and water supply to attract small, medium and large-scale businesses. He also proposed simplifying business registration and permit processes, eliminating multiple and arbitrary levies within the state’s jurisdiction and improving the regulatory environment to attract domestic and foreign investors. On electricity, Odii said his administration would leverage the opportunities provided by the Electricity Act 2023 to attract private investment into power generation and distribution. He listed solar mini-grids, biomass, gas-based power solutions and other renewable energy sources as options for improving electricity supply to industrial clusters, commercial centres and underserved communities. On infrastructure, he promised investments in roads, housing, water supply and digital connectivity, with particular emphasis on linking agricultural production areas to industrial clusters, storage facilities and markets. For the education sector, Odii pledged free public primary and secondary education, improved school infrastructure, better teaching quality and expanded access to practical and technical education. He also proposed partnerships with educational institutions, manufacturers and industry associations to strengthen vocational training and equip young people with skills required by emerging industries. In healthcare, the manifesto promises improvements in medical infrastructure, staffing, access to essential medicines and the quality of healthcare delivery, particularly in underserved communities. On security, Odii advocated a coordinated, intelligence-led and community-based approach to tackling kidnapping, communal conflicts, cultism, drug abuse and other criminal activities. He specifically identified the longstanding communal disputes involving Abaomege and Ishinkwo, Ezza and Ezilo, Ezza and Effium, as well as Ngbo and Agila, as conflicts requiring sustained intervention and peaceful resolution. The proposed approach includes stronger collaboration among security agencies, traditional rulers, local governments and community organisations, alongside improved intelligence gathering, surveillance and emergency response mechanisms. The PDP candidate also promised institutional reforms covering land administration, right-of-way permits, the civil service and judicial administration. On funding, he said his administration would conduct a comprehensive assessment of the state’s financial position, existing obligations and development priorities while strengthening internally generated revenue without imposing unnecessary burdens on residents and businesses. He proposed public-private partnerships, development financing, community development partnerships and infrastructure tax incentives as alternative funding mechanisms. The manifesto also promises transparent procurement processes, digital budgeting, expenditure tracking and regular publication of reports on government revenue and expenditure. On implementation, Odii pledged to develop a detailed execution plan for the proposed initiatives and pursue visible results within his first 200 days in office if elected. He also promised to establish a delivery unit to monitor government commitments and ensure accountability for measurable outcomes. The manifesto presents his vision of making Ebonyi a preferred investment destination through inclusive economic growth, sustainable wealth creation and improved living standards.
